reading.rtitle: Follow-up note -- Q3 board meeting, two weeks on
paras: Two weeks after the board meeting, five actions are on the tracker and two of them are still outstanding. The Houston budget is closed: the board signed off on it on Thursday, and nothing further is needed from anyone on this note.

The supplier quote has not arrived. Procurement is carrying a three-week backlog after the holiday, so this is a queue problem rather than a decision problem. I am going to chase it up today, and if the quote is not with us by Friday the installation date is going to slip by a fortnight.

The contract review is the real bottleneck. Legal has not moved on it for two weeks, and everything downstream is waiting for that one signature. I have already sent one nudge and made one call. I am meeting counsel at nine on Thursday, and I have told her plainly that if the review has not moved by Friday afternoon I will escalate it to the board, so that nobody is surprised when it appears on the agenda.

Two smaller points. The Houston site visit is booked: I am meeting the local team at nine on Thursday the fourteenth. And on the insurance renewal, which has not started, we are going to loop in counsel before we reply to the broker. Finance and I will touch base on Wednesday. Please reply to this note only if a date on it is wrong.

gist.prompt: What is this note mainly about?
choices: A complaint about how slowly the legal department works
Where each action from the meeting stands, and what happens next on the two that are late
A request for the board to approve the Houston budget

items: The Houston budget still needs approval.
The board signed off on it on Thursday, and nothing further is needed.
The supplier quote is late because of a decision nobody has taken.
It is a queue problem: procurement is carrying a three-week backlog after the holiday.
The writer will escalate the contract review without warning anyone first.
She has told counsel plainly that she will escalate on Friday, so that nobody is surprised.
The Houston site visit already has a date and a time.
She is meeting the local team at nine on Thursday the fourteenth.
Counsel will be brought into the insurance renewal before the broker gets a reply.
We are going to loop in counsel before we reply to the broker.

listenings.text: Good morning. This is the status of the five actions from the board meeting, in order. Item one, the Houston budget: closed. The board signed off on it on Thursday and there is nothing outstanding. Item two, the supplier quote: late. Procurement is carrying a three-week backlog after the holiday, so nobody has refused anything, the request is simply sitting in a queue. I will chase it up this afternoon. Item three, the contract review: this is the real bottleneck. Legal has not moved for two weeks and everything else is waiting on that signature. If it has not moved by Friday I am going to escalate it to the board. Item four, the Houston site visit: booked. I am meeting the local team at nine on Thursday the fourteenth. And item five, the insurance renewal, which has not started. We are going to loop in counsel before we reply to the broker, and finance and I are touching base on Wednesday. Two items outstanding, one bottleneck, no surprises.

I want to say something about the sentence I will look into it, because it is the most expensive sentence in corporate English. It has no owner and it has no date. The person who writes it thinks they have promised something. The person who reads it does not know whether it is a decision, an intention, or a very polite no. So in every action item I write, there are three things and never fewer: a verb, an owner and a date. And the tense does real work there. If I decided it on the call, while I was speaking, I write will. I will chase it up this afternoon. If the plan already existed before I opened my mouth, I write going to. We are going to loop in counsel, as we agreed on Monday. And if the thing is already arranged, with a person and a time in the diary, I use the present continuous. I am meeting counsel at nine on Thursday. One last habit, and it is the one that keeps relationships. Before I escalate anything, I nudge once, I chase up once, and I tell the owner the exact date on which I am going to escalate. Nobody has ever been angry with me for escalating. They get angry when it is a surprise.

extra_audio.text: First, you write the action item properly: a verb, an owner and a date, so nobody can read it two ways. Then, a few days later, you send a friendly nudge to the owner, because most things are simply sitting in a queue. After that, if nothing arrives, you chase it up and you find out what the real bottleneck is. Next, you warn the owner: you say the exact date on which you are going to escalate, so that nothing is a surprise. Finally, if the date passes, you escalate to the person above, you loop in whoever needs to see it, and you update the tracker so the board reads the same story you do.
